sessions.title: Given, Not Chosen
sessions.aim: To turn from the self we manufacture to the self we receive: identity as gift rather than achievement, grounded in the image of God, and to follow Augustine's restless heart to the discovery that the rest we've been chasing was never going to come from inside us.
sessions.summary:
After two sessions inside the exhaustion, this one names the alternative, and it isn't a better technique for making a self. It's the end of self-making. The deepest thing about you was given, not chosen. Before you defined yourself, you were made in the image of God, and that image isn't a grade you earn but a dignity you carry because you were made. It isn't at stake in any performance and can't be lost in any failure.

Isn't that just a holier version of the same trap, one more thing to live up to? The church has often preached it that way, as a standard to perform. But in Genesis the image is a status given at creation, true of you before you'd done anything and true of you on your worst day.

Augustine, after years of building a self from ambition, pleasure, and reputation, began his Confessions with this prayer: "You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you." The restlessness we try to cure by building a better self is a homing signal. We can't achieve our way to what we most need, because it was always a gift, and a gift can't be earned without ceasing to be a gift.

keyScripture.why: "So God created man in his own image" (Genesis 1:27). Human worth is given at creation, not achieved. It's an identity bestowed before any performance, carried on the best day and the worst alike.

discussion.q: What's the difference between an identity you receive as a gift and one you build as an achievement? Which have you been living on?
discussion.behind: This is the central distinction. Most people have lived on the achievement model without naming it. Help them feel why a gift can't be earned or lost, which is exactly the rest the performed self never reaches.

discussion.q: Being made in God's image is true of you on your worst day. Where do you find it hardest to believe your worth isn't at stake in how you perform?
discussion.behind: Most people affirm the image of God in theory and live as if their worth is on the line every day. Help people find where the gift feels unbelievable, in failure, comparison, or shame, so the teaching reaches the place it's actually needed.

discussion.q: Has "you're made in God's image" sounded to you like rest, or like one more thing to live up to? What made the difference?
discussion.behind: The church has often preached the image as a demand. Let people say where they heard it that way, so they can hear it fresh as a status given rather than a standard imposed.

discussion.q: Augustine prayed, "You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you." Where do you feel that restlessness? Have you ever noticed it pointing somewhere instead of just nagging?
discussion.behind: Reframe chronic dissatisfaction not as a problem to fix by building a better self but as evidence of what the self was made for. Help people feel the restlessness as a clue rather than a curse.

discussion.q: Read 1 John 3:1. Where have you been trying to earn what can only be received? What would it cost you to stop?
discussion.behind: Go first. The hardest thing for the self-made is to stop earning, because earning feels like control and receiving feels like helplessness. Name that honestly.

objections.objection: Saying I'm made in God's image just swaps one impossible standard for a holier one. Now instead of living up to my potential I have to live up to being God's image-bearer. How is that rest?
objections.response: The church has often preached it exactly that way, and that version is crushing; you're right to flinch. But look at what the image actually is in Genesis. It isn't a goal set in front of the human being. It's a status given at the moment of creation, before the first person had done anything, good or bad. You don't earn the image by behaving like God's representative. You bear it because God made you to. You bore it the day you were born, and you bear it on your worst day, and you can't perform your way up to it or fail your way out of it. That isn't a higher bar. It takes the bar away from the question of your worth entirely. If a gift has to be lived up to, it has been turned back into a wage, which is exactly the trap the teaching was meant to free you from.

objections.objection: This sounds like a comforting story to quiet the anxiety. How is a given identity any more real than a self-made one? Both are frameworks. At least with the self-made one I'm honest that I'm building the meaning.
objections.response: That's the sharpest form of the objection, and it deserves a straight answer. You can't prove the image of God the way you prove a theorem, and I won't pretend it's a deduction. But the alternative is in the same position. A self-made identity is also a framework, also unproven, also a story, and it has a testable consequence: the self has no ground but its own construction, so it can't give you rest. A thing that holds itself up can't also be held. So the question isn't which story is provable; neither is. It's which story fits the evidence of your life, including the restlessness no achievement quiets and the emptiness after the applause. The self-made story can only say you haven't built well enough yet. The given story says you're tired because you were made to be held and have been trying to hold yourself. You're right that you're constructing the meaning. The question is whether the constructing is what's wearing you out.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your worth was settled at creation by God's act, not by anything you've done or failed to do, what's the one thing you've been working hardest to prove that you could finally put down?
sessions.practice: This week, practice receiving instead of achieving. Each morning, before you do anything that could earn or lose anyone's approval, say out loud: "I am made in the image of God. This is true of me before I've done anything today, and it will be true tonight no matter how today goes." Through the day, notice each time your mind reaches to earn your worth back, through performance, comparison, or self-justification, and return to the morning's sentence. On a day you fail at something that matters, do it most of all. Read Augustine's prayer slowly, and write down whether calling your restlessness a homing signal instead of a defect changed how you carried it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've been trying to earn what you already gave. We've treated our worth as a project, building it and defending it and watching it wobble, when you settled it at creation by making us in your image, before we'd done anything to deserve it or forfeit it. Forgive us for turning your gift into a wage, for hearing "image-bearer" as a standard to reach instead of a name to rest in. You've made us for yourself, and our hearts have been restless, and we've tried to cure the restlessness by building a better self, when it was a signal pointing home to you. Teach us to receive what we can't earn. Quiet the striving. Let us rest tonight in being made and named by you. Amen.
reflection: Have I been living on an identity I receive as a gift or one I build as an achievement? What does my exhaustion say about which one I've trusted?
Where is it hardest to believe my worth was settled at creation? What would change if I believed it there?
What is my restlessness pointing toward? Have I been trying to quiet a homing signal by building a self instead of coming home?
sessions.teaching:
We've spent two sessions inside the exhaustion of the self-made life, and tonight we turn toward the alternative. But I need to say first what the alternative isn't, because the obvious guess is wrong. The answer to the exhausting project of making yourself isn't a better project of making yourself: a more spiritual technique for building a stronger self, "look inward and find yourself" with God added as a motivational resource. If that's what you came for, the study should disappoint you. The answer is the discovery that you were never meant to make a self at all.

The deepest thing about you was given, not chosen. Before you ever turned inward to define yourself, you'd already been defined, from outside, by the act of a Maker. The Bible names it on its first page with a phrase we've heard so often we've stopped hearing it: "So God created man in his own image" (Genesis 1:27).

That phrase has been worn smooth by repetition, and often misused, so let's recover what it says. The image of God isn't an achievement. It isn't a goal, a standard, or a level of holiness you reach by trying hard. It's a status, given to you at creation, before you'd done a single thing to deserve it or lose it. You bore it the day you were born, helpless and accomplishing nothing. You bear it on your worst day, having failed at everything that matters to you. No performance raises you up to it, and no failure knocks you out of it. And God's word over his creation came before anyone had done anything at all: "God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). That takes the question of your worth off the table. Your dignity isn't recalculated each morning from yesterday's results. It was settled, once, by God.

Here the skeptic in the room has a right to object, because this is where the church has often gotten it wrong. We've taken this gift and turned it back into a job. We've preached "You're an image-bearer, so act like one," with the unspoken threat that if you don't, you're failing at the one thing you were made for. That's a betrayal of the teaching. It takes a status given and turns it into a wage demanded. It produces exactly the same exhaustion as secular self-making, just with holier words, which may be worse, because now even your relationship with God is a performance you might fail. If you've heard "image of God" as one more impossible thing to live up to, hear me: that isn't the gospel. The image isn't what you must become. It's what you already are.

Augustine saw this disease more clearly than anyone. As a young man he did what our age commands. He looked everywhere for himself and built an identity out of intellect, ambition, pleasure, and reputation, and under all of it he found a restlessness nothing he built could quiet. At the start of his Confessions, written around AD 400, he prays the sentence that diagnoses the human condition: "You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you."

That reframes everything. The chronic dissatisfaction, the sense that you aren't yet who you should be, the emptiness that survives every success: Augustine says that isn't a problem to solve by building a better self. It's a signal. It's the soul's evidence that it was made for a rest that can't come from inside the self, because the self is the very thing that's restless. We've spent our lives misreading it as a sign we haven't built enough yet, when it's always been a sign that we were made for a rest we can only receive.

That's why self-making fails. It doesn't fail because you're building badly or haven't found the right technique. It fails because it's the wrong kind of thing. You were never meant to be self-made. You were meant to be made, named, and given to yourself by another. A creature trying to be its own creator isn't working too little. It's attempting the one thing it can't do: hold itself up. The exhaustion is the sign of a project that was impossible from the first day.

So here's where this session leaves us, quietly and heavily. You can't achieve your way to the thing you most need, because the thing you most need was always a gift, and a gift can't be earned. The moment you earn it, it becomes a wage, something you're owed and could lose, which is the very anxiety you were trying to escape. "See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are" (1 John 3:1). That has to be received with open, empty hands. For many people the hardest thing about faith isn't believing God exists. It's believing the deepest thing about them could be a gift. To stop achieving and start receiving feels at first like helplessness, like giving up control. It is. And it's the beginning of rest.

scriptureStudy.note: "So God created man in his own image." The image is given at creation, before any achievement. Human worth is a gift received, not a project built.

"And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good." God's judgment over creation, the human included, comes before the human has done anything. It's the original approval the performed self keeps trying to earn from the crowd.
"You formed my inward parts ... Your eyes saw my unformed substance." The self is known and made by God before it can know or make itself.
"For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works." We're the thing made, not the maker. Even the good we do flows from an identity given, not the other way around.

"See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are." Identity as gift, named plainly: a status the Father's love gives, received and not earned.
"Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God." A creature's worth rests on God's regard for it, not on its productivity or display.

"Will what is molded say to its molder, 'Why have you made me like this?' Has the potter no right over the clay?" The creature receives its form from its Maker, which undercuts the demand to be the sole author of oneself.

sessions.goingDeeper:
A group that wants to go further can read more of Augustine's Confessions, because the restless heart is much richer than its famous sentence. The book is partly the story of a brilliant, ambitious man who looked for meaning in philosophy, sex, status, and achievement and found each unable to bear the weight he put on it. His diagnosis wasn't only that he'd chosen bad things, though some were. It was that he'd looked for rest in created things, including his own self, when rest could only come from the Creator the self was made for.

That's a claim about human nature: we're made facing God, with a built-in reference to something beyond ourselves, so any attempt to find our rest inside our own boundaries contradicts our design. Set that beside the buffered self from session 1 and feel the collision. The buffered self is exactly the attempt to be self-enclosed, and Augustine says in advance that it can't work, not because of a rule but because of what we are.

Notice too how this turns the restlessness from a defect into a mercy. If the heart could rest in lesser things, it would, and it would never come home. On Augustine's account, the inability of any achievement to satisfy is grace in disguise, a signal that won't let the soul settle for a counterfeit. The discipline is to read your own dissatisfaction theologically, hearing in the ache of the self-made life not a demand to build more but an invitation to receive what you were made for.

memoryVerse.text: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.

sessions.title: In Christ
sessions.aim: To move from the image of God shared by every person to the new identity given to those united with Christ, the name that holds when the performance fails, and to recover baptism as the public naming of a self received rather than achieved.
sessions.summary:
The image of God settles the worth of every human being. This session goes further, to the identity Scripture says is given to those joined to Christ, because the deepest answer the faith gives to "Who am I?" isn't a quality inside you but a location outside you: in Christ.

Paul's most startling claim about himself isn't that he became his best self, but that his old self died. "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me" (Galatians 2:20). "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3).

Doesn't that mean losing yourself into a religious collective, the very crushing of the person the modern self rightly feared? It's the strongest objection there is. But union with Christ isn't erasure. What dies is the performing self that has to justify its own existence. What rises is you, finally given ground to stand on. Baptism is the naming of that change: "buried therefore with him by baptism into death" so that "we too might walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:4). Martin Luther is remembered for steadying himself in his worst hours with a fact done to him, "I am baptized." There's a name that holds when everything you built collapses, and you didn't make it.

keyScripture.why: "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me" (Galatians 2:20). Paul's identity has moved off the performing self and onto union with Christ.

discussion.q: Paul says the deepest answer to who he is isn't a quality inside him but a location outside him: in Christ. Why might an identity anchored outside yourself be steadier than one held inside?
discussion.behind: An identity held inside the self rises and falls with the self's performance. One anchored outside it doesn't. Help people feel why worth located in Christ doesn't move when they do.

discussion.q: Read Colossians 3:1-4. What would it mean for your truest self to be hidden somewhere safe, instead of always on display and at stake?
discussion.behind: "Hidden" is a relief to the performed self, which has to display everything. A hidden identity isn't a lost one. It's a protected one, out of reach of the audience's verdict.

discussion.q: Some fear that belonging to Christ means losing yourself in a religious crowd. Where do you feel that tension? How might belonging to Christ and being yourself not be opposed?
discussion.behind: Take the fear seriously; it's the strongest objection our age has on this point. Then let people feel the turn: union with Christ doesn't dissolve the self but grounds it. Don't resolve it too fast.

discussion.q: Read Romans 6:3-4. When your performance and feelings give way, what fact do you return to? What would it mean to have one?
discussion.behind: The performed self has only feelings and performance to fall back on, and both fail. Help people feel the difference between an identity grounded in something done to you and one grounded in how you're doing. That's why baptism can be such a sturdy anchor.

discussion.q: Where have you watched a self you built collapse: a role, an achievement, a relationship that carried who you were? What would it have meant to have a name underneath it you couldn't lose?
discussion.behind: Go first. Everyone has had a built self collapse. You're after the recognition that the selves we make can be lost, and the longing for one that can't.

objections.objection: Losing myself in Christ sounds exactly like the crushing of the individual the modern world fought to escape. You spent the first session defending the protest against being forced into a mold, and now you want me to dissolve into a religious identity. That's the mold again.
objections.response: It's right to fear the erasure of a person. The faith has sometimes done exactly that, and the protest against it is one the prophets would sign. But union with Christ is the reverse of erasure. What dies in "I have been crucified with Christ" isn't your personality, your gifts, or your particular you. It's the performing self, the self that has to justify its own existence, the exhausting author-and-audience self of session 2. What rises isn't a generic religious unit. It's you, finally on a foundation solid enough that you can stop defending yourself and become who you were made to be. Think of the most distinctive people you've known. They're usually the least anxious about proving their individuality, because their worth is settled and they're free to be themselves. Union with Christ doesn't pour you into a mold. It takes you out of the one mold that was really crushing you: having to earn your own worth.

objections.objection: Telling people their real self is "hidden with Christ" sounds like a way to avoid their actual life and problems. It's escapism, retreating into a spiritual identity instead of facing who you are and doing the work of becoming better.
objections.response: It can be abused that way, and the church has sometimes enabled the dodge. But the reality runs the other direction. Most people can't face who they really are, their failures, patterns, and shameful parts, because their worth is riding on the outcome, so honest self-examination feels like a threat to their whole identity. The person whose identity is hidden with Christ, settled and not at stake, is the one finally free to look at themselves honestly, because the looking can no longer destroy them. Your worst trait, fully admitted, can't lower a worth that was never based on your traits. The performed self has to hide its failures to protect its worth. The self hidden in Christ can confess them freely. That isn't escapism. It's the only ground from which real truthfulness and real change are possible.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your truest self were really hidden with Christ, safe and settled and out of reach of any judgment, what part of your life would you finally be free to face, that you've been hiding because facing it felt like it would destroy you?
sessions.practice: This week, learn to return to the fact rather than the feeling. When the performance fails, when you fall short, when the old anxiety about your worth rises, return to something done to you rather than something you produced. If you've been baptized, say it: "I am baptized. I've been buried with Christ and raised with him, and that's true however today went." If you haven't, return to the fact of what Christ has done for you. Each morning read Colossians 3:3, and through the day, whenever you feel your identity rise or fall with your performance, say quietly, "My life isn't here, on display and at stake. It's hidden, safe, in him." Write down what that does to your anxiety.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've built so many selves and watched them fall: the role that ended, the achievement that faded, the image that cracked. Each time it felt like we were falling with them, because we were standing on them. Thank you that in Christ you've given us a name we didn't make and can't lose, and that our life is hidden with Christ in you, out of reach of the audience and the verdict and even our own failure. Forgive us for living as if our worth were on display when you've hidden it in your Son. When our performance gives way, and it will, teach us to return to the fact: we're yours, baptized into Christ, crucified and raised with him. Let us stop defending a self we built and rest in the one you gave. Amen.
reflection: Is my identity held inside me, rising and falling with my performance, or anchored outside me in Christ? What does my anxiety say about which I'm standing on?
What would change if I believed my truest self were hidden with Christ, safe and settled, instead of always on display?
When my performance and feelings give way, what do I return to? What would it mean to have a name done to me that I couldn't fail my way out of?
sessions.teaching:
The image of God, which we looked at last time, is the dignity of every human being, settled at creation, true of every person whatever they believe. Tonight we go further, to the new identity the faith says is given to those joined to Christ. I want to begin with the most startling thing Paul ever wrote about himself, because it cuts against everything our age teaches us to want.

Our age says the answer to "Who am I?" is a quality inside you: the true self, the inner core. Paul says the answer to who he is isn't inside him at all; it's a location outside him. "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me" (Galatians 2:20). And to the Colossians, stranger still: "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3). Paul isn't saying he improved himself or found his true inner core. He's saying his old self died, and his real life, his truest identity, is now somewhere else: hidden, in Christ, in God. The center of who he is has moved outside him. That's the deepest answer the Christian faith gives to the question of identity. It isn't a quality you possess. It's a union you've been brought into.

The modern self will object at once, and the objection deserves its full weight. This sounds like erasure. It sounds like the crushing of the individual into a mold that session 1 honored people for refusing, the dissolving of a hard-won self into some religious mass where nobody is anybody. "It is no longer I who live" can sound like the slot to end all slots. If that's what union with Christ meant, the modern world would be right to fight it, and I'd fight it too.

But the claim is the reverse. What dies in "I have been crucified with Christ" isn't your personality, your gifts, your humor, the particular and irreplaceable you. It's the performing self, the exhausted author-and-audience self of session 2, the one that has to justify its own existence and defend its own standing every day. That self, and only that self, is crucified, and its death isn't a loss. That self was never the real you. It was the prison you were trapped in. What rises on the other side isn't a generic believer with your name filed off. It's you, standing for the first time on a foundation solid enough that you don't have to hold yourself up. Think of the most unmistakably themselves people you've known. They're almost never the ones working hardest to be individuals. They're the ones whose worth is settled, so they're free to be odd and unimpressive and exactly who they are. That's the freedom union with Christ gives.

Then hear the word "hidden" again, because it's a mercy the performed self can barely imagine. The performing self has to put everything on display, its worth visible and verified, nothing safe. Paul says your truest self has been taken off the stage and placed where the audience can't reach it, the verdict can't touch it, and even your own failure can't get at it: kept in God himself. That isn't a lost self; it's a protected one. It can't be canceled, exposed, or lost, because Christ holds it and not your performance.

The church has a word for the moment this move is declared, and it may be the most underused identity word we have: baptism. We've shrunk baptism into a ceremony, a box checked, and lost what it is. Paul says, "We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:4). Baptism is first something done to you, a name spoken over you, a fact about you that doesn't depend on how you feel on a given morning. That's why it can hold in the worst storms. Martin Luther suffered spells of self-accusation and dread so severe he could barely function, and he's remembered for steadying himself with the words "I am baptized." Not "I feel forgiven," because often he didn't. Not "I've done well enough," because he was sure he hadn't. But a fact done to him, outside him, that stayed true when his feelings and his performance had both collapsed.

You've watched selves collapse. We all have: the role that ended and took your sense of who you were with it, the achievement that faded, the relationship that defined you and then was gone. When a self you built collapses, it feels like you're collapsing, because you were standing on it. The promise of union with Christ is that under every self you built there can be a name you didn't build: given in Christ, anchored in what he did and not in what you do, hidden in God where no failure, no audience, and no death can reach it. When we fail, and we will, we can learn slowly to do what Luther did: stop reaching for a feeling or a performance to save us and return to the fact. I am his. That holds.

scriptureStudy.note: "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me." Identity moves off the performing self and onto union with Christ: the old self-justifying self dead, and a new life received rather than produced.

"For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God." The truest self is hidden and safe, out of reach of the audience and the verdict, secure because it isn't riding on the visible performance.

"Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death." Baptism names a relocated identity, buried and raised with Christ, a fact done to us.
"Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come." "In Christ" marks where the new identity lives: given, not achieved.
"He chose us in him before the foundation of the world ... he predestined us for adoption." The new identity rests on God's choice before we existed, settled before any performance could touch it.

"But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession." Identity is named in the plural and given by God's choosing: belonging that grounds the self instead of dissolving it.

"To the one who conquers ... I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it." The final identity is a name Christ gives, the deepest self bestowed rather than built.

sessions.goingDeeper:
A group that wants to go further can look at union with Christ, the center of Paul's thinking about identity, which the modern church has often let shrink into sentiment. "In Christ," "in him," and "in the Lord" appear well over a hundred times in Paul's letters. They aren't decoration. They name the basic reality of a Christian's existence: that the believer's standing, righteousness, life, and identity aren't qualities held in themselves but realities held in Christ and shared by being joined to him.

The Reformers, especially John Calvin, made this central. In the final edition of his Institutes (1559), Calvin taught that as long as Christ remains outside us, all he suffered and did for our salvation is of no use to us; we must be united to him (paraphrased). Our righteousness isn't our achievement but his, received by faith and held in him, which is exactly why it can't be lost by our failure or earned by our performance.

Notice how directly that answers the exhaustion this study has traced. The performed self has to produce and defend its worth because that worth is located in itself, on display and at stake. Union with Christ moves the worth entirely, so it's held in another and isn't riding on daily performance. The buffered self of session 1 is sealed and self-contained; union with Christ takes down that very wall and grounds the self outside itself, which the buffered self experiences as a threat and is in fact its rescue. Then weigh baptism as the sign and seal of that union: not a work the believer performs but a word God speaks.

memoryVerse.text: For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.

sessions.title: The Self Poured Out
sessions.aim: To end where the whole study has been heading, with the paradox that the self is found by being lost, and to show that an identity secure enough not to need defending is finally free to be spent in love rather than performed for approval.
sessions.summary:
The study ends on the hardest and most freeing thing Jesus said about the self: "For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it" (Mark 8:35). Our age says save the self: build it, protect it, express it, put it first. Jesus says the self you clutch is the self you lose, and the self you give away is the self you find.

Isn't that just self-erasure, a call to be a doormat? The worry is serious, because this verse has been used to push people into codependent self-abandonment and even back into danger. That was never Jesus' teaching. The losing he means isn't erasing the self but loosening the grip, and only a self that's already secure can let go. That's why this session comes last. You can't pour out a self you're still desperately trying to fill.

A performed self can't afford to lose itself; it has nothing underneath, so even its service is a bid for approval. A self whose worth is settled in Christ can finally be spent without fear, because there's nothing left to protect. Christ himself "emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:7). The study doesn't end with a self admired. It ends with a self spent, and finds that's the self that was truly found.

keyScripture.why: "For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it" (Mark 8:35). Jesus reverses the self-saving instinct: the clutched self is lost, and the secure self is free to be spent.

discussion.q: Where have you seen that clutching something tightly, a relationship, a reputation, control, cost you the very thing you were trying to keep?
discussion.behind: Most people have watched grasping for security lose it. Help the room see the paradox isn't abstract but observable, so they're ready to hear why the self given away is the one found.

discussion.q: You can't pour out a self you're still desperately trying to fill. Why do you think this session had to come last? What happens when people try to "lose themselves" before their worth is secure?
discussion.behind: People who serve from an empty, unsecured self are still performing, still bidding for approval, and they burn out or grow resentful. Real self-giving comes from a self already settled in Christ.

discussion.q: "Lose your life" has been used to pressure people into self-abandonment. How is what Jesus means different from that, and why does the difference matter?
discussion.behind: This is pastorally serious. Distinguish loosening the grip on a secure self from abandoning a self that was never secure; the first is freedom, the second a wound. Protect anyone in the room who has been pressured into self-erasure in God's name, and name the difference clearly. If someone is being harmed now, make a private way to talk and help them find real help.

discussion.q: Where have you served or given in a way that was secretly a bid for approval? How did you know?
discussion.behind: Go first, gently. Much of our giving is performance in disguise: service that needs to be seen and thanked. This isn't a guilt trip. It helps people see why only a secure self can give without keeping score.

discussion.q: Read Philippians 2:5-8. Looking back over all five sessions, what would actually change in your week if you lived from a given identity instead of a performed one?
discussion.behind: Move the whole study from idea to life. Have each person name one concrete change in how they'd work, serve, or rest. Let it land as invitation, not assignment, and leave it with weight rather than a bow.

objections.objection: "Lose your life" and "pour yourself out" sound like a recipe for being used up, letting everyone walk over you, having no boundaries and no self. People have been spiritually abused with this exact verse. Why isn't this just codependence with a Bible verse?
objections.response: This shouldn't be waved away. The verse has been weaponized, used to push abused people back into danger and to shame people out of legitimate self-protection, and anyone wounded that way deserves to hear it called what it was: abuse, not the teaching of Jesus. Here's the distinction everything turns on. Losing a self that's secure is worlds apart from abandoning a self that was never secure, and only the first is what Jesus means. The codependent self-abandonment that destroys people isn't the free pouring out of a settled self. It's the desperate emptying of an unsettled one, a person with no foundation trying to earn worth or safety by disappearing. That isn't love. It's fear wearing love's clothes. That's why this is the last session and not the first. You can't freely lose a self until you have one secure enough to lose, hidden in Christ, nothing left to protect. Losing your life in Jesus' sense requires first having found it in him. The order is everything, and reversing it is the abuse.

objections.objection: The whole study built up a secure identity, and now you're telling me to give it away. That feels like a bait and switch. Why would I let go of the security you just gave me?
objections.response: It would be a bait and switch if security were the destination. It was never the destination; it was the foundation. Our age treats a secure self as the finish line, something to achieve and then enjoy, and a self that exists only to enjoy its own security is, in the end, small and lonely. Notice that you don't let go of the security by pouring yourself out. You use it. You can spend yourself on others without fear because your worth is settled in Christ and can't be drained, so giving doesn't lower it. A self that has to protect its worth has to hoard it, can't risk it on love, and stays curved in on itself. A self secure in Christ is the only self that can afford to forget itself. You're not being asked to give the gift back. You're being shown what it was for.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your worth were so settled in Christ that you had nothing left to protect, who is the one person, and what is the one act of love, you'd pour yourself into that you've been holding back because you couldn't afford to?
sessions.practice: This week, practice what only a secure self can do: love that keeps no score. Choose one act of real self-giving toward someone who can't repay you or thank you adequately, and do it without telling anyone, with no return possible, to feel the difference between serving for approval and serving from security. Watch the part of you that wants credit, and instead of feeding it, remember that your worth is already settled in Christ and doesn't need this to be seen. Each morning read Mark 8:35 and Galatians 2:20 together. Looking back over all five sessions, write down the one concrete way you most want to live from a given identity rather than a performed one, and name the first step.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we came into this study tired of building a self, and you've shown us a self we didn't have to build: made in your image, given in Christ, hidden safe in you, a name we can't lose. Now, at the end, you ask the hardest and most freeing thing, that we let it go, not because it isn't precious but because it's so secure it can finally be spent. Teach us the difference between losing a self that's safe in you and abandoning one that was never secure, and protect anyone here who has been wounded by that confusion. Free us from giving that's secretly a performance, love that keeps score, service that needs to be seen. Settle our worth so deeply in your Son that we forget ourselves at last and pour ourselves out, and find that the self we gave away was the one we were looking for. Amen.
reflection: Where has clutching a self, to save it, protect it, or prove it, cost me the very thing I was trying to keep? What would it mean to loosen the grip?
How much of my serving and giving has been a bid for approval rather than love that forgets itself? What does that say about where my worth is anchored?
Looking back over all five sessions, what would change in my ordinary week if I lived from an identity given in Christ instead of one I have to perform?
sessions.teaching:
We end where the whole study has been heading, on the hardest and most freeing thing Jesus said about the self: "For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it" (Mark 8:35). Hear how completely that reverses the instruction we've lived under. Our age says save the self: build it, protect it, express it, put it first, because losing it is the great catastrophe. Jesus says the self you clutch and try to save is exactly the self you'll lose, and the self you give away is the one you'll find.

The modern ear raises an objection here, and it isn't cheap. In many rooms it's a wound. "Lose your life" sounds like self-erasure: having no self, being a doormat, letting everyone walk over you in the name of holiness. I have to be careful here, because this verse has been weaponized. It's been used to push abused people back into danger, to shame the wounded out of any self-protection, to tell someone being destroyed that their destruction is godly. That isn't Jesus' teaching. It's abuse wearing his words. If you've been hurt that way, hear me plainly: what you were told was a lie, and Jesus never said it.

So here's the distinction everything turns on. Losing a self that's secure is worlds apart from abandoning a self that was never secure, and only the first is what Jesus means. The self-abandonment that destroys people, the disappearing, the having no boundaries, isn't the free pouring out of a settled self. It's the desperate emptying of an unsettled one, someone with no foundation trying to buy worth or safety by vanishing. That isn't love. It's fear in love's clothing, and it leaves a person more enslaved.

That's why this session comes last. You can't freely lose a self until you've found one secure enough to lose. You can't pour out a self you're still desperately trying to fill. The performed self of session 2 can't afford to lose itself, because there's nothing underneath. So its "service" is secretly another performance, another bid for the approval it needs to survive. An unsecured self can't give. It can only invest, hoping for a return. That's why so much religious service curdles into resentment and burnout: it was the performed self trying to earn its worth through good deeds, keeping a secret ledger, needing to be seen and thanked. A self that needs to be thanked hasn't given anything. It's made a purchase.

Most of us know that ledger. We've served and needed it noticed. We've given and waited for credit. We've done the right thing and felt quiet resentment when nobody saw, which is the surest sign the giving was about us. Love poured out from a secure self doesn't keep score, and ours was counting.

But here's the good news. A self whose worth is already settled, hidden in Christ, anchored in what he did, can finally be spent without fear, because there's nothing left to protect. When your worth is secure in Christ and can't be drained, giving yourself away doesn't diminish you, because what you're giving isn't your security. That's held by another. So for the first time you're free to love, to forget yourself, to serve the person who can't repay you and won't thank you, to do good in secret with no return, because you no longer need anything from anyone.

That's the shape of Christ himself. "Though he was in the form of God, [he] did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:6-7), all the way to a cross. He could pour himself out completely because he was completely secure, the eternally beloved Son. A worth that settled has nothing to defend and everything to give. And union with him is what makes the same pouring out possible, slowly, in us. "By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers" (1 John 3:16).

So I won't tie this in a bow. We came in tired of building a self, told we had to invent ourselves, look inward, perform, and win the room's approval forever, and we found it was bondage dressed as freedom. We found that the deepest thing about us was given: we're made in God's image, our worth was settled at creation, and in Christ we've been given a name we can't lose, hidden in God. And now we find that the point of all that security was never a secure self to admire. It was a self secure enough to spend. The self-made age produces a self that has to be performed, anxiously, forever, and never finds itself. The given identity produces a self that can be poured out freely in love, and finds in the pouring what it was looking for all along. The self you finally stop clutching, because it's already safe in him, isn't the self you lose. It's the only self you ever truly find.

scriptureStudy.note: "For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it." The great reversal: the self clutched is lost, and the self spent is found.
"Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit." The self that protects itself remains alone; the self poured out bears life.

"Though he was in the form of God, [he] did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself." Christ pours himself out from complete security as the Son, the model of a secure self spent in love.

"It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me." The union behind the pouring out. A self spent in love isn't self-erasure but Christ's own self-giving life lived through a self secure in him.
"For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul?" The self-saving project is exactly what loses the self.
"My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." A secure self can admit weakness without threat, because its worth is held in Christ and not in its own strength.
"By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers." Our self-giving rests on Christ's self-giving first.

sessions.goingDeeper:
A group that wants to go further can look at the paradox of finding yourself by forgetting yourself, because it's the deepest collision between the gospel and the self-made age, and it's a claim about how the self actually works. Our age assumes the way to a fulfilled self is to attend to the self, and that turning toward others is a cost the self pays. Jesus and the whole Christian tradition say the opposite: the self curved in on itself, always checking its own state and worth, is the unhappy self, and the self is found and made glad precisely in forgetting itself, its attention turned outward toward God and neighbor.

Martin Luther, following Augustine, described sin as the heart "curved in on itself" (in Latin, incurvatus in se). That names the disease: a self so preoccupied with itself it can't rest or love freely, which is exactly the condition of the performed self in session 2, endlessly monitoring its own reception.

That reframes the whole study. The point of a secure identity in Christ isn't a self that finally feels good about itself, a holy self-esteem, because a self focused on its own feelings about itself, even good ones, is still curved inward. The point is a self so secure it can stop thinking about itself and forget itself in love. Ask whether the endless modern work of feeling good about oneself is just another form of the exhausting self-focus this study has described, and whether the gospel offers something deeper than higher self-regard: freedom from needing to regard the self at all.

leaderPrimer:
Every small group is an audience, and an audience is exactly what the people in this study don't need one more of. They live before audiences all day: the feed, the workplace, the mirror, the inner critic keeping score. The risk over these five weeks is that your circle of chairs becomes another stage. Watch for it. Someone will confess their exhaustion with performing in a way that's itself a performance, polished, likable, well timed, and you mustn't reward the polish. Reward the fumble instead: the half sentence that goes nowhere, the admission that comes out ugly, the person who says they don't actually know who they are. That's the study working, and the room has to learn that nobody here is grading.

It learns that from you, which is inconvenient, because leading is a performed role too, and you'll feel the pull to be impressive in a study about the tyranny of being impressive. Refuse it in the first ten minutes. Say early, in your own words, where your own worth still rides on the room.

Be fair to "be true to yourself" in session 1. It isn't stupid. It freed people from real tyrannies, and half your room got free of something through it. Honor that before the study counts its costs, or nobody will trust the counting. Be careful in session 5, too. "Lose your life" has been used to push people into self-abandonment and even back into harm; if anyone in your group is being harmed now, make a private way to talk and help them find real help.

And be patient with the turn to gift. People who've carried the project of themselves for decades don't set it down on a Tuesday because Galatians was mentioned. They set it down in rooms where, for one hour, nothing they say is being scored. Build that hour. Let your group be the one place all week where everyone is off the market: nothing to sell, nothing to audition for. That hour is the study.

faq.q: Is this study going to make me feel guilty about how much I curate and perform myself?
faq.a: No, and it works hard to prevent that. The whole series treats the performed self not as a character flaw but as the reasonable behavior of someone told their worth is something they produce and display. If anyone leaves more ashamed of their performing than when they came, the study has failed. If you came braced to be told you're vain, you'll find a study that stands in the exhaustion with you and treats your tiredness as the place to start, not the failure.

faq.q: What does it mean that the modern self was "invented"? Isn't the self just what a person is?
faq.a: Session 1 walks through this. The claim isn't that human beings are new but that a particular way of understanding the self is recent: the inward, self-defining individual who looks inside for the answer to who they are and treats their feelings as the truest thing about them. Charles Taylor traces how the West came to experience the self as "buffered," sealed off from God and any larger order and drawing its meaning from inside its own walls. Robert Bellah named the working creed of that self "expressive individualism," the belief that each person has a unique inner core to discover and express. The point isn't that this is simply wrong but that it's one answer, recent and debatable, not a fact of nature. Once you see the inward turn as a habit you were trained into, you can ask whether there's a deeper foundation underneath it.

faq.q: "Be true to yourself" is good advice, isn't it? Why would a study question it?
faq.a: The study honors what's good in it before questioning anything. "Be true to yourself" carries a real protest: refusing to be crushed into a mold by family, church, or culture, and defending a person's one irreplaceable life. That protest is closer to the prophets than its critics usually realize. The question the study raises isn't whether the self matters but which self you're being told to be true to. If the inward self was shaped all the way down by the same culture that told you to look inside, then being true to it isn't standing on bedrock. It's standing on a floor someone built and calling it the ground. The study doesn't despise the instruction. It asks whether it can bear the weight we've put on it.

faq.q: Why is being yourself so exhausting? I thought it was supposed to be freeing.
faq.a: Session 2 is built on this question. Being told to invent yourself sounds like freedom until you realize there's no final version. The self has to be continually built, defended, updated, and presented, and because a self with no foundation outside itself can't approve of itself, you have to watch the audience to see if it's landing. You become two people, the author writing the self and the audience watching to see if it sells, and both jobs run all day. The exhaustion isn't a sign you're doing it badly. It's the built-in cost of a self that has to be earned and re-earned every day. The study reads that tiredness as a message: a soul made to be given an identity, trying instead to manufacture one.

faq.q: If my worth comes from being made in God's image, isn't that just a higher standard to live up to?
faq.a: Session 3 answers this directly, because the church has often preached it that way. But the image of God isn't a goal set in front of you. It's a status given at creation, true of you before you'd done anything and true of you on your worst day. You don't earn it by behaving like God's representative; you bear it because God made you to, and no performance raises you to it and no failure knocks you out of it. That isn't a higher bar. It takes the bar away from the question of your worth. If a gift has to be lived up to, it's been turned back into a wage, which is exactly the trap the teaching was meant to free you from.

faq.q: Does losing yourself in Christ mean losing your individuality and becoming a generic religious person?
faq.a: Session 4 takes this worry seriously, because it's the strongest objection our age has on this point, and the answer is the reverse of what the fear assumes. The self that dies in Paul's "I have been crucified with Christ" isn't your personality, gifts, or particularity. It's the performing self that has to justify its existence and earn its worth every day. What rises isn't a generic religious unit but you, finally on a foundation solid enough that you can stop defending yourself and become who you were made to be. The most distinctive people you've known are usually the least anxious about proving it, because their worth is settled. Union with Christ doesn't pour you into a mold. It breaks the one that was crushing you.

faq.q: What does baptism have to do with identity?
faq.a: Session 4 recovers baptism as one of the most underused identity words the church has. We've shrunk it into a ceremony you complete and lost what it is: a naming, the public declaration that your identity has been relocated, "buried ... with him by baptism into death" and raised to "newness of life" (Romans 6:4). It's first something done to you, a fact that doesn't depend on how you feel on a given morning, which is why it can anchor the soul in a storm. Martin Luther, in his worst spells of self-accusation, is remembered for steadying himself with the words "I am baptized": not "I feel forgiven," because often he didn't, but a fact done to him that held when his feelings and his performance both collapsed.

faq.q: The study builds toward a secure identity and then session 5 tells me to give it away. Isn't that a bait and switch?
faq.a: It would be, if security were the destination. It was always the foundation. Our age treats a secure self as the goal, which leaves a settled self turned inward, admiring itself, a small and lonely thing. The study claims the security was always for something: a self whose worth is settled in Christ and can't be drained is the only self that can afford to forget itself and be spent in love without keeping score. You don't give up the security by pouring yourself out. You use it.

faq.q: I've heard "lose your life" used to pressure people into self-abandonment. How is this different?
faq.a: Session 5 names that abuse plainly and refuses it. The verse has been used to push the abused back into danger and to shame people out of legitimate self-protection, and anyone hurt that way was hurt by an abuse of the verse, not by Jesus. The difference is between losing a self that's secure and abandoning a self that was never secure, and only the first is what Jesus means. Codependent self-abandonment isn't the free pouring out of a settled self. It's the desperate emptying of an unsettled one, a person with no foundation trying to earn worth or safety by disappearing, which is fear in love's clothing. That's why this is the last session and not the first. You can't freely lose a self until you've found one secure enough to lose. The order is everything, and reversing it is the abuse. If you're being harmed now, please talk to someone safe and get help.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't "given identity" just a comforting story to replace a harder truth?
faq.a: That's a fair challenge, and session 3 answers it head on. You can't prove the image of God like a theorem, and the study won't pretend you can. But the alternative is in the same position: a self-made identity is also a framework, also unproven, and its consequence is that the self has no ground but its own construction and so can't give you rest. The real question isn't which story is provable but which fits the evidence of your life, including the restlessness no achievement quiets and the emptiness after the applause. The self-made story can only say you haven't built well enough yet. The given story says you're tired because you were made to be held and have been trying to hold yourself. The study asks you to weigh the two fairly, not to pretend.

faq.q: Why does the study keep asking the leader to admit their own performing instead of just teaching the answer?
faq.a: Because the whole study is about the end of performance, and a leader who performs a settled identity he doesn't have has already contradicted the message and turned the leading into one more show. You can't lead a tired, performing person out of the trap from above them without your help turning into shame or distance. A leader who says, "I perform too; I clutch selves that collapse too," can sit beside the room as a fellow learner, which is where real teaching about identity comes from.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I haven't got my own identity figured out?
faq.a: That may be your best qualification. The study is built to be led by a fellow learner, not by someone who has it all settled and hands out security to the anxious. Every discussion question has a note behind it, every objection has a response, and every session ends in prayer, so you aren't improvising. Being truthful about where your own worth still rides on the room, the work, or the role may be the most freeing thing in the room. What you do need is to refuse to shame anyone, keep the room safe for the exhausted and the skeptical, protect the wounded especially in session 5, give the skeptic's objections their full strength, and point everyone, yourself first, to the One who made us in his image and gives us a name in Christ we can't lose.

timeline.event: Genesis opens Israel's Scriptures by grounding human identity in being made in the image of God, not in self-definition. The deepest thing about a person is given at creation.
Paul writes Galatians ("I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live") and Romans, describing identity as union with Christ, named in baptism.
Paul writes to the Colossians, "your life is hidden with Christ in God," placing the truest self in Christ, safe, rather than on display and at stake.
Augustine writes the Confessions, the story of a self that tried to make itself and failed, opening with the prayer "You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you."

Martin Luther, battling crushing self-accusation, recovers the believer's identity as a gift received rather than a performance achieved, and is remembered for steadying himself with the words "I am baptized."
John Calvin's Institutes of the Christian Religion (first edition 1536, final edition 1559) makes union with Christ central: what Christ did benefits us only as we are united to him.
Robert Bellah and colleagues publish Habits of the Heart, naming the working creed of the modern American self "expressive individualism."
Charles Taylor publishes A Secular Age, describing the "immanent frame" and the "buffered self."
Social media turns the audience's verdict into a visible, countable, real-time number, intensifying the anxious self-display that was already part of the modern self.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here. There's almost nothing harder to talk about truthfully than the self we've been building and defending. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can say here, "I don't really know who I am underneath all this." You can say, "My whole worth is riding on my work," or "I got everything I performed for and felt nothing," or "I'm tired of being myself." Nobody's going to grade you or hand you a tip to fix it. Second, this study isn't a better technique for building a stronger self. It's about discovering that you were made and named before you ever started building, and that your worth was given, not earned, and can't be lost. Third, I'm in this too. I've measured my worth by the reaction in a room and gone home empty. We're not teaching identity from above. We're learning it together. Tonight we're sitting with this part of the question "Who am I?": ________. I'll read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone says anything.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what this passage says about who we are. Now let's bring it home, off the page and into the week we're about to walk into, the work and the rooms and the quiet moments where we actually build a self or set one down, because that's where this either matters or doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, and if it doesn't feel resolved, that's fine. Receiving an identity and spending it is the work of a life, not one evening. Take this into your week. Try the practice, and sit with the reflection questions on your own. And if you're carrying a self that's already collapsed, or a worth riding on something that can't hold it, or a wound from being told that having no self was holiness, please don't carry it alone. Talk to me or to someone safe in this room. Let me pray for us before we go. Thanks for being willing to tell the truth tonight.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and shame, and say plainly that everyone in the room has been building a self and is more tired than they admit, and that this room is safe for that.
Week 2: Session 1, The Buffered Self, taking care to give "be true to yourself" a fair hearing before questioning it.
Week 3: Session 2, The Exhausting Project of Self-Creation, with extra time on performing and the audience, handled without contempt.
Week 4: Session 3, Given, Not Chosen: the image of God and identity as gift, and Augustine's restless heart as a homing signal.
Week 5: Session 4 part one, In Christ: identity moved off the performing self and onto union with Christ.
Week 6: Session 4 continued: baptism, the name done to you that holds when feeling and performance give way.
Week 7: Session 5, The Self Poured Out, with great care for anyone wounded by pressure to erase themselves.
Week 8: Bringing it together. Walk back through the five sessions and practices, and name what each person is carrying out of the study, with space for anyone who needs further help.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together: the invented self and the exhaustion of performing it.
Week 2: Session 3, Given, Not Chosen, with extra time on Augustine's restless heart.
Week 3: Session 4, In Christ: union with Christ and baptism, with care for anyone whose built self has collapsed.
Week 4: Session 5, The Self Poured Out, with a short closing time walking back through all five sessions.

glossary.definition: Charles Taylor's term for the modern self, sealed off from any larger order and drawing its meaning from inside its own boundaries. The study treats it as one recent understanding of the self, not the natural human condition.

Taylor's name for the modern experience of the world as a closed natural system with no window onto anything above it, so that meaning, if any, must come from inside. It's what makes looking inward seem like the only option.
Robert Bellah's name for the working creed of the modern self: each person has a unique inner core of feeling and intuition that must be discovered and expressed, and doing so is the point of a life.
The claim of Genesis 1:27 that human beings are made in God's image, understood here not as a standard to perform but as a status given at creation: a dignity no one can earn or lose.
Augustine's description of the soul's chronic dissatisfaction ("our heart is restless until it rests in you"), read in this study as a homing signal toward a rest the self can't manufacture.
The study's central claim: the deepest thing about a person is given, not chosen, received from God in creation and in Christ rather than assembled by the self.

A self with no foundation outside its own performance, which has to be built, defended, and shown to an audience whose verdict it needs to feel real. The source of the exhaustion described in session 2.

Paul's "in Christ": the believer's standing, life, and worth held not in themselves but in Christ and shared by being joined to him, so identity rests outside the self and can't be lost by the self's failure.
Identity grounded in baptism understood as a naming, a fact done to the believer that they've been buried with Christ and raised with him. An anchor that holds when feeling and performance fail.
The self that, secure in Christ, is free to be spent in love rather than performed for approval. The found self of Mark 8:35, discovered by being given away.
The freedom of a self so secure in Christ that it can stop attending to its own worth and turn outward in love, the opposite of the heart "curved in on itself."

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Our age handed everyone one instruction and called it freedom: look inward, find your true self, define yourself on your own terms, then perform that self for the world's approval. For many it's become hard labor, being your own author and your own audience at once, with no day off and no final version. This five-session study looks at where that idea of the self came from, why it's so exhausting, and the older answer it replaced: identity not as something you assemble but as a gift you receive. You're made in the image of God, given a name in Christ you can't lose, and secure enough at last to spend yourself in love. It takes the tiredness and the skeptic's questions seriously, and it never shames people worn out by performing. Any volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Come tired, not finished.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on identity: the question "Who am I?" and the exhausting answer our age keeps giving, build a self and perform it for approval forever. Before anyone braces, hear this. It won't shame you for how much you perform, and it won't hand you a holier technique for building a better self. It's about discovering that you were made and named before you ever started building, and that your worth was given and can't be lost. No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. If you're tired of being yourself, this is for you. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: Our age told you to look inward, build a self, and perform it for approval forever, and it's exhausting. A five-session study on who you are: stepping out of the project of making yourself and into an identity you didn't have to manufacture and can't lose, made in God's image and given a name in Christ. It takes the tiredness and the skeptic's questions seriously. Come tired, not finished.
quoteCards: The self you're told to be true to has a history. It's a floor someone built, and you're being told it's the ground.
You become two people at once: the author writing the self and the anxious audience watching to see if it sells.
The exhaustion isn't a sign you're building the self badly. It's a sign you were never meant to build one.
Your worth was settled at creation, by God's act, not recalculated each morning from the day's results.
You can't achieve your way to the thing you most need, because the thing you most need was always a gift.
There's a name that holds when everything you built collapses, and you didn't make it.
When his performance and his feelings gave way, Luther returned to a fact done to him: "I am baptized."
You can't pour out a self you're still desperately trying to fill.
The self you finally stop clutching isn't the self you lose. It's the only one you ever truly find.
Not the self you were sold. The self you were given, and then freely gave away.
